newsitem.title: USA: Judge says du Pont jury has trouble reaching verdict.
newsitem.headline: Judge says du Pont jury has trouble reaching verdict.

text.p: Jurors in the murder trial of millionaire chemicals heir John du Pont were clearly struggling as they ended a fifth day of deliberations on Saturday with no verdict, and Judge Patricia Jenkins said she hoped they were not confused.
The district attorney overseeing du Pont's prosecution said he believed a hung jury was unlikely and said there were signs the jury had ruled out an acquittal by reason of insanity.
"I'm encouraged that we're going to get a result," Delaware County District Attorney Patrick Meehan told reporters on Saturday afternoon. "I'm not concerned about a hung jury at this point in time."
"This jury is working at this," he said. "They appear to have an internal resolve to continue to push to try to get a resolution."

Asked whether it seemed likely by their questions to the court that the jurors had ruled out an insanity verdict, Meehan said, "Based on their requests, one might conclude that they've ruled out insanity."
Du Pont is charged with first- and third-degree murder as well as voluntary manslaughter in the Jan. 26, 1996 killing of Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.
Du Pont's lawyers have conceded that du Pont killed Schultz, but they are seeking an insanity verdict, saying he was unaware of the wrongfulness of his acts.
Jenkins, addressing a late-afternoon jury request for office supplies and for an early end to the day's deliberations on Saturday, said it was evident they were having trouble reaching a verdict.
"Clearly you have had this case for many hours over several days. You are having, or are apparently having, some difficulty resolving some of the issues in the case," Jenkins said.
She said the difficulty was a positive in that it reflected seriousness on the part of the six-man and six-woman jury.
But she added, "Hopefully it is not the result of confusion you have in your minds about the instructions on the law or how the law applies to the facts that you have in this case."
Jenkins granted the jurors' request for marking pens, an easel board, notepads and tape.

She declined to let the jury adjourn immediately, but reversed plans to keep them late into the evening and sent them back to their hotel at the usual time of 6 p.m. The jurors are to have a day off on Sunday and resume on Monday for deliberations.
Relatives of several jurors were seen bringing suitcases into the Delaware County courthouse earlier Saturday as the jurors' sequestration, which began Tuesday, dragged on.
The jury is faced with eight possible verdicts in the case.
The jury can find du Pont not guilty or not guilty by reason of insanity on all of the charges, or guilty or guilty but mentally ill on any one of the three homicide counts.

Before they began their deliberations on Saturday, jurors heard another legal explanation from Jenkins, who, responding to a jury request, read for the fifth time the legal definition of first degree murder.

But the focus of the jurors' questions has steadily narrowed, and the latest request made no mention of third degree murder and voluntary manslaughter charges the jurors asked about on previous occasions.
